n: In this lecture we consider questions connected with resuscitation and transplantation. At the end of the 20th century, resuscitation, transplantology and other medical technologies developed rapidly. For this reason the question of recording the death of a human being passed from a purely medical problem into the category of bioethical problems. Supportive therapy and organ removal need an answer to one question: which state of the organism is recognised as the moment of death? Another aspect is that donor organs are in serious shortage. In the USA and Europe, transplantation is not available to about 35 percent of those in need.

The lecture plan is as follows. First, the types of transplantation and the medical and ethico-legal restrictions are considered. Then the brain death criterion and the procedures for removing organs from the dead are studied, that is, presumed consent and presumed refusal, where the word "presumption" means an assumption made in advance. Then organ shortage, organ allocation, commercialisation and the attitude of various religions are covered. In this order we go from types and medical restrictions to the views of religions.

First we define the basic concept. Transplantation is the transfer of an organ or tissue from one organism to another. The person from whom the organ or tissue is taken is called the donor, and the person to whom it is transplanted the recipient, that is, the receiver. Transplantation is usually divided into experimental and clinical. Note that experimental transplantation is a preclinical stage in which biological, surgical and organisational problems are worked out.

Now we compare experimental and clinical transplantation. Transplantation is the transfer of an organ or tissue from one organism to another, and is usually divided into experimental and clinical. Experimental transplantation is the preclinical stage: here biological, surgical and organisational problems are worked out. After transplantation, the immune state of the recipient is studied and new preparations that help engraftment are developed. In this way the transition is made from experiment to clinical transplantation.

We classify the types of transplantation by who the donor is. The donor may be the recipient himself, his twin, another person or an animal. Auto- is autologous, allo- is homotransplantation, and xeno- is also called interspecies transplantation. In autotransplantation the donor is the recipient himself, for example healthy skin is transplanted to a burned area. In isotransplantation an identical twin, that is, a genetically identical person, is the donor. In allotransplantation the donor is a genetically different person, and in xenotransplantation an animal of another biological species. In leukaemia and lymphoma, after high-dose chemotherapy, bone marrow or stem cells are autotransplanted.

t: Attention: do not confuse auto- and isotransplantation
n: Let us pin down a place where mistakes are often made. Auto-: the recipient himself is the donor. For example, in a severe burn, skin from an undamaged area is transplanted to the burned area. Iso-: the donor is another person, that is, an identical twin, immunologically and genetically identical to the recipient. Allo-: the donor is another person who differs genetically and immunologically. Xeno-: the donor is an animal of another biological species. Attention: auto- is not equal to iso-, and allo- is not equal to xeno-. The difference lies in who the donor is: himself, a twin, another person or an animal.

Now we consolidate with quick questions. First situation: in leukaemia, after high-dose chemotherapy, the patient's own bone marrow cells were transplanted. Which type is this? In the second situation an organ from the recipient's identical twin was transplanted. In the third situation an organ from a pig was transplanted into a person. Which types? Remember: auto is oneself, iso is a twin, allo is another person, xeno is an animal of another biological species. The risk of error here: isotransplantation, that is, a twin, differs from allotransplantation, that is, another, genetically different person.

Let us consider the case analysis. A severely burned patient had skin taken from his undamaged areas transplanted to the burned areas. In the second case a patient with leukaemia received high-dose chemotherapy, and then his own bone marrow or haemopoietic stem cells were transplanted back. To the third recipient the organ was given by an identical twin; they are immunologically and genetically the same. Question: which type does each case belong to, and who is the donor? Why does the problem of finding a donor differ for these types? Think about these questions.

The restrictions on transplantation fall into two groups. Medical factors include immunological matching, the recipient's health and immunosuppressive therapy. That is, the donor is matched immunologically and the recipient's health indicators are assessed. Ethico-legal restrictions include confirmation of death, removal and allocation of organs, and commercialisation. The greatest difficulties are connected precisely with ethical and legal problems. Commercialisation means subordinating the activity to the aim of making a profit.

t: The living donor and the "do no harm" dilemma
n: We turn to the living donor. Removal of an organ from a living donor involves harm to the donor's health. Here a dilemma arises: harm to the donor or the life of the recipient, that is, the person receiving the organ; there is no choice but to select one. This dilemma is resolved by weighing benefit against harm. The rule is this: the benefit must always exceed the harm. That is, when an organ is taken from a living donor, harm is done to health, but the benefit obtained must be greater than this harm.

Now removal of organs from the dead, that is, cadaveric donation. Removal of organs and tissues from a dead body is the most widespread kind of donation. It is precisely this kind that is connected with a number of ethical, legal and religious problems. There are three main problems: confirmation of death, that is, when it is recorded that the person has died; voluntary refusal, that is, refusal to donate an organ after death; and religious permissibility, that is, use of the body from the standpoint of religion. Solutions are given in documents at the international, national and confessional, that is, religious, level.

t: Living and cadaveric donation: main differences
n: We summarise the main differences between living and cadaveric donation. Removal of an organ from a living donor involves harm to his health; the physician cannot fully observe the rule of "do no harm". The dilemma is resolved by weighing benefit against harm: the benefit obtained must exceed the harm done. Removal of organs from a dead body is the most widespread kind of donation; it is connected with ethical, legal and religious problems. The circle of living donors is determined by the law of each state: they may be close relatives or non-relatives.

t: Case analysis: choosing a living donor
n: Case analysis: choosing a living donor. The patient's life depends on an organ transplant. His brother is ready to be the donor, and so is a close acquaintance. A living donor may be a close relative, for example a brother or parent, or a non-relative, for example a friend or acquaintance; the circle is determined by law. First question: in both cases harm is done to the donor. How is the rule "benefit must exceed harm" applied here? Second question: why is the legal circle important when a non-related donor is chosen? What is weighed in making the decision?

t: Determining death: a bioethical, not a medical, problem
n: We return to the determination of death. At the end of the 20th century, resuscitation and transplantation technologies developed. For this reason, confirming the fact of death became not a purely medical but a bioethical problem. Measures to sustain life and to remove organs need a clear answer to one question: which state of the organism is recognised as the moment of death? Many of the ethico-legal problems of transplantation are connected with recording death, extracting the organ, allocation and commercialisation. Do not err: in the living donor the main dilemma is the rule of "do no harm", and in the dead donor the problem of confirming death.

t: Resuscitation: terminal states and clinical death
n: We consider terminal states from the standpoint of resuscitation. Preagony lasts from several minutes to several days: consciousness is clouded, arterial pressure falls, and breathing and circulation are disturbed. In the terminal pause breathing suddenly stops and the pupil dilates; it lasts from several seconds to 3–4 minutes. Clinical death begins after the heart stops, usually lasting up to 5–6 minutes; at low temperature it may extend to 30 minutes. The possibility of restoring function in clinical death became the basis for the emergence of the science of resuscitation.

We consider the concept of brain death. Brain death is the destruction of the whole brain with irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes. This concept was developed after the description of coma dépassé; it was described by the French neurologists Mollaret and Goulon. The brain is a delicate system that artificial systems cannot replace. Its destruction is understood as death. That is, brain death is confirmed when irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes occur together and the whole brain has perished.

Quick questions on brain death. First question: name the three signs of brain death. Answer: irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of spontaneous breathing, loss of brainstem reflexes. Second question: what is the chief criterion of human death in many countries? Answer: brain death; it is confirmed in legislative acts. In 1968 the Harvard criteria of brain death were developed; in the same year, in a refined form, they were recognised by the world medical community. Attention: cessation of spontaneous breathing alone does not mean brain death; in the definition the signs come together and with destruction of the whole brain.

t: History of brain death: Mollaret, Goulon, Harvard
n: The history of the idea of brain death. The French neurologists Mollaret and Goulon described coma dépassé; from this came the concept of brain death. Brain death is irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes. In 1968 the Harvard criteria were developed, and the Declaration of Sydney of the World Medical Association, that is, the WMA, recognised them. As a result, this idea was enshrined in laws as the criterion of death.

t: Case analysis: resuscitation and brain death
n: Case analysis: resuscitation and brain death. A patient in resuscitation has irreversible loss of consciousness, no spontaneous breathing, and loss of brainstem reflexes. Breathing and circulation are maintained by machine. Question: is this state death? In most countries brain death is recognised as the chief criterion of human death. Attention: loss of consciousness alone is not enough. Cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes are also required. Ruling of the Islamic Fiqh Academy, 1988: removal of organs is permitted from a person with brain death whose breathing and circulation are artificially maintained.

t: Brain death: definitions in two textbooks
n: Two textbooks give brain death a different emphasis. In the bioethics textbook, brain death is destruction of the whole brain with irreversible loss of consciousness, cessation of spontaneous breathing and loss of brainstem reflexes. In the forensic medicine textbook, death of the cerebral cortex is the beginning of biological death and is accepted as "brain death". Between death of the cortex and death of other organs there is an interval of about 20 hours; removal of organs is based on this. Brain death is determined in the procedure laid down by the Ministry of Health, usually by resuscitation specialists and neurologists.

The question of euthanasia and stopping resuscitation. The term "euthanasia" was introduced in the 16th century by F. Bacon; its original meaning is relieving the suffering of a terminally ill patient. Direct active euthanasia is homicide or suicide; in the indirect form there is no aim of hastening death. Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, is limitation or cessation of aid; in criminal law it counts as failure to perform official duty. Medicothanasia relieves suffering with drugs; dysthanasia prolongs life to the maximum by palliative and radical methods.

t: Three ways of removing organs from the dead
n: There are three ways of removing organs from the dead. In the old way, the body is considered the property of the state; the state has the right to use organs as needed and for scientific purposes. Presumed consent is adopted in countries such as Austria, Belgium, Spain, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Presumed refusal is applied in the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy; in the USA there is a donor card. That is, under presumed consent removal is possible if refusal has not been expressed, while under presumed refusal a document of consent is needed during life.

t: Presumed consent and presumed refusal (A and B)
n: Let us place presumed consent and presumed refusal side by side. Under presumed consent, a person who objects must express the objection in the established manner. Consent is taken as given in advance, and if there is no document it gives the right to remove the organ. Under presumed refusal, a person who agrees must formalise the consent in the established manner. Refusal is taken as existing in advance, and if there is no formal consent the organ is not removed; the donor card in the USA may be named as an example. Attention: these two concepts are opposite. Silence counts as consent in one and as refusal in the other.

Let us consider the practice of states and legislation. In nearly 40 states, programmes are regulated by sections of the Constitution or by special laws. National laws rely on international norms on the rights, freedom and protection of the person. Presumed consent operates in Austria, Belgium, Spain, Hungary and the Czech Republic: if refusal has not been expressed, removal is possible. Presumed refusal operates in the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy: without legal consent it is not possible. At the basis of all the documents lie the principles of informed voluntary consent and social justice.

Case analysis: presumption in practice. In situation A, a person died. During life neither he nor his relatives had declared to a health-care institution any refusal of organ removal. In situation B, the deceased, his relatives or his legal representative had notified the institution of refusal. Question: in a country with presumed consent, is there a right to remove organs in cases A and B? And under presumed refusal? The guide is as follows: under presumed consent the right is given in case A and not given in case B. Under presumed refusal, without legal consent removal is not possible.

A quick question on the types of presumption. What does "silence" mean in removing an organ from a deceased person? The answer depends on the type of presumption, that is, assumption. Under presumed consent, if refusal has not been expressed in advance, the right to remove the organ is given; so in Austria, Belgium, Spain, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Presumed refusal is also called "requested consent": without formal consent the organ is not removed. It operates in the USA, Germany, Canada, France and Italy. Attention: do not mix up these two concepts. In one, refusal must be declared; in the other, consent.

t: Shortage of donor organs and ways to resolve it
n: Shortage of donor organs and ways to resolve it. In both the USA and Europe, about 35 % of those in need do not live to transplantation. The first way: people are urged to formalise consent during life and to give organs voluntarily. The second way is technological: an artificial organ, cell culture and animal donation are being sought. An artificial organ may be mechanical, connected with bioelectronics and nanotechnology. In cell culture, tissue is obtained from a somatic stem cell. In animal donation, ways of obtaining animal organs are studied.

On artificial organs. The "artificial kidney" apparatus is widely used in medical practice. In cardiac transplantology, artificial heart valves have begun to be used. Artificial joints and lenses of the eye are also used. Artificial organs have begun to solve the problems of shortage and of removal of organs from a living or dead donor. However, this path requires large economic expenditure, scientific research and trials. It depends on the achievements of engineering, chemistry and biology.

We consider the advantages and problems of xenotransplantation. The pig is in the lead as a donor: its chromosomes and organs are close to human ones, it breeds quickly, and it is a domestic animal. There are two main problems: transmission of infections and viruses, and compatibility of the animal organ with the human. In addition, animal protectionists object. A person's accepting an animal organ as his own may also be a psychological problem. As a solution, a human gene is introduced into the pig genome, a transgenic pig is obtained, the organ is transplanted to the human, and the likelihood of rejection is reduced.

Therapeutic cloning and stem cells. Therapeutic cloning is the possibility of producing donor organs and tissues by means of genetic technologies. The chain of the idea is as follows: a stem cell culture is obtained from a human somatic cell, tissue is grown in artificial conditions, and the person himself becomes both donor and recipient. This is ethically favourable: there is no need to open the body to remove an organ, and there is a chance to solve the compatibility problem. It is still at the experimental stage: cartilage and muscle tissues are being tested; introduction into practice is still far off.

t: Allocation of organs and waiting lists
n: Allocation of organs and waiting lists. A waiting list is a list of patients who need an organ transplant; health characteristics are stated in it. The patient is entered on the list, the order is set by the principle of justice, the immunological compatibility of the organ is checked, and if a suitable organ is found, the operation is performed. Remember: even a seriously ill patient who is first in line may not reach operation because of immunological incompatibility. Improving immunosuppressive therapy partly solves the problem, but it remains topical.

Commercialisation of transplantology. Commercialisation is subordinating an activity to making profit; in it a human organ becomes a commodity. In shortage, an organ becomes a very expensive commodity. In many countries the buying and selling of organs is prohibited by law. Nevertheless demand creates a black market, and the seller-donor most often sells a kidney. This is contrary to the idea of humanism: in transplantology death should serve to prolong life.

Quick questions on allocation and trade. First question: what is a waiting list, and on which principle is it based in allocating organs? Second question: what is commercialisation? Why does a black market arise in shortage? Attention: first place on the list does not guarantee operation, because immunological compatibility is also needed. Remember: "demand gives rise to supply". This economic law explains the existence of a black market.

Case analysis: shortage and trade. A living person, because of material hardship, decided to sell one of his kidneys. The buyer is a patient waiting on the list. First question: removal of an organ from a living donor involves harm to his health. How is the principle of "do no harm" violated here? Second question: assess this transaction from the standpoint of the principles of voluntary consent and social justice. Is the consent really voluntary? Third question: Islam strictly prohibits trade in organs, and the Orthodox Church opposes regarding an organ as an object of purchase and sale. Why?

t: International documents and religious views: Christianity
n: International documents and views in Christianity. In 1987 the World Medical Association adopted a declaration on organ transplantation. It sets out the conditions for confirming death and ethical principles; the physician cares for the health of the person. In Orthodoxy trade is impossible, sacrifice is voluntary, and risk to the donor's life is inadmissible. In Catholicism donation is mercy and a moral duty, possible when there is no alternative treatment. In Protestantism the legitimacy of the organ obtained is recognised, and sale of organs is immorality. Attention: Orthodoxy rejects presumed consent; Catholicism regards donation as mercy.

Views on transplantation in Judaism and Buddhism. In Judaism the human body is treated with great respect even after death; the body of a dead person must not be cut open. Removal of an organ is possible only if the person gave permission before dying and the family does not object. Special attention is paid to ensuring that the donor's body is not mutilated. When it is a matter of saving a human life, Judaism regards transplantation of organs as permissible. In Buddhism, an organ may be transplanted only from a living donor. The sole condition is that it must be a gift to the sick person.

t: Islam: Resolution No. 26 of the Fiqh Academy
n: Islam: Resolution No. 26 of the Fiqh Academy. In 1988 Resolution No. 26, 1/4 was adopted. The first rule: the expected benefit must clearly exceed the possible harm. Vital organs are prohibited; the living donor must be a Muslim and must give consent. In brain death, if breathing and circulation are artificially maintained, it is permitted. Commerce, however, is strictly forbidden.

Case analysis: religious approaches. The organs of a patient with confirmed brain death may save the life of another patient. How do religions regard this? In Judaism removal of an organ is possible with the prior permission of the deceased and no objection from the family. In Islam the donor or his relatives must consent. The Catholic Church calls donation mercy and a moral duty. The Orthodox Church regards it not as an obligation but as voluntary self-sacrifice. Attitudes to trade are similar: the Orthodox reject it as the buying and selling of organs, Protestants call it immorality, and Islam strictly forbids it.

t: New problems: genome, patent, solidarity, UNESCO
n: We consider new problems. The organs of transgenic pigs with an introduced human gene should reduce the likelihood of rejection. In xenotransplantation the problems are transmission of infections and viruses, and compatibility; the ethical questions are animal rights and the feeling of being human. On the question of inequality, the technologies are expensive for developing countries, and this is a question of solidarity, that is, unity. The genome is the "heritage of humanity"; the committee proposed financing the technologies from part of the income. UNESCO, that is, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, made ethics a priority in its 2002–2007 strategy.

We conclude the lecture. Types of transplantation: auto-, iso-, allo- and xenotransplantation. Removal of organs from the dead is the most widespread donation and gives rise to the most ethico-legal problems. In many countries the criterion of death is brain death. Removal from the dead is carried out in the old way or by presumed consent or presumed refusal. Shortage: in the USA and Europe about 35 percent of those in need cannot obtain an organ. Solutions: artificial organs, xenotransplantation, therapeutic cloning. Principles opposing commercialisation: do no harm, informed voluntary consent, social justice. Religions condemn trade, and many permit voluntary donation.
